turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'm Sister Nkosi, I'll just do your obs before the doctor calls you in. Hop up on the bed for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, thank you. We got a bit flustered, the robot on the M4 was hectic and then there was no parking by the rooms.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Ag you're fine, we're running behind anyway. My sister was stuck at that same robot for ages this morning fetching her child from school, so I know how it goes.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Right. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over eighty-two, pulse is seventy-six, temperature thirty-six point eight, and your oxygen is ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp. I always go stiff when that cuff tightens.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Howzit, I'm Doctor Naidoo. Sorry about the wait. What's brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this pain, up on the right under the ribs, on the stomach side. It comes after I eat fatty food and then it sits there for hours.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. Take me through it, how long it's been and what kicks it off.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, it started about six weeks ago, the week after my niece's birthday braai, I had boerewors and potato salad with mayo, and about an hour later this ache started right under the right rib, not the left. It built and it stayed, I'd say three hours, maybe a bit more, and I couldn't get comfortable sitting or lying. It's happened again, I think four or five times since, always after something rich.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, she's actually sore every single day, even if she just eats a salad. She won't tell you the half of it.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag no, that's not how it is. It's not every day, a salad I'm fine with. It's the fatty stuff, the vetkoek, the chops, the creamy pasta, and on ordinary days I go to work and I'm ok.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): When that pain is on you, do you get nausea, vomiting, any fever?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Nausea, ja, a bit, that heavy feeling. Vomiting only the once, err, two weekends ago after a plate of vetkoek from the church fete, I brought it all up and then the pain carried on a couple of hours and eased. No fever, I checked with the thermometer at home and it was normal.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was white as a sheet that night. I was ready to drive her to casualty.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I was shaky, ja, but it passed. I took my antacid and eventually I slept.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which antacid are you using, and how much?

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): It's Gaviscen, the liquid, the mint one. I take, umm, I think it's ten mil when the pain starts, and sometimes I repeat it if it's still sore, not every day, only when I've been silly with the food. It takes the edge off a little, it doesn't really kill it.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any yellowing of the eyes or the skin? Dark urine, pale stools?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Urine is the normal yellow, stools are brown, same as always. I checked my eyes in the car mirror because my husband kept saying I looked off, and they're white.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the rest of the gut, bowels, any heartburn? Waterworks, your periods?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Bowels are regular, once a day, no diarrhoea and no constipation. Heartburn, well, I get a bit of acid sometimes but that's old, years, not this pain. Waterworks is fine, no burning, and my periods are still regular, I'm forty-six.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, medicines or foods?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none that I know of. I've had penicillin before, no rash or anything.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Family history, anyone with gallstones, diabetes, blood pressure?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes, picked up in his fifties, he was on tablets till he passed, and my mother did not have diabetes, she was proud of that, but she did have her gallbladder taken out about ten years back, same kind of pain after fatty meals she said. Another sister, the one in Joburg, not the one who stays with my mom, she has pressure, high blood pressure, but no sugar, they checked her and the sugar was fine.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): And for yourself, any operations, any ongoing illnesses? Work, hours, what you eat, exercise, smoking, drink?

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations, I've never been under the knife, and I don't have diabetes or pressure myself, the clinic checked last year. I'm an accounts clerk at a freight company down at Bayhead, I start at half past seven and I'm usually out by five, sometimes six if month-end piles up, so about ten hours. Diet is a problem if I'm honest, I love a braai with boerewors and chips, and in the week I grab vetkoek or a pie at the tuck shop because there's no time, and exercise is basically nothing besides the walk from the car to the office. Alcohol is a glass of white wine on a Friday and maybe a Saturday, and I don't smoke, never have, not even when I was young.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in, doctor. The urine dip from earlier is clear, no blood, no sugar. If I yawn, my little one was up the whole night with an earache.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks, sister. Lie back for me, I just want to feel your tummy.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): There's tenderness right under the right rib margin when I press, and it catches when you breathe in, so Murphy's sign is mildly positive. The tummy is soft otherwise, no guarding. Your eyes aren't yellow, the sclera are clear.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, that spot. That's exactly where it grabs me, shame.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): So, thinking out loud, pain after fatty meals, lasting hours, your mom's gallbladder, that tender spot, it points me towards biliary colic, stones in the gallbladder. I'm not going to conclude that today though. It could also be a stomach ulcer or just gastritis from the rich food, and I won't rule those out until we've looked. When you eat fat the gallbladder squeezes to push bile out, and if a stone is sitting in the neck you get that grinding pain for a few hours, that's the mechanism I'm picturing, not something we've proved.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So you think it's the same as my mother? She was in hospital three days and she said the gas afterwards was worse than the stones, and I've been worrying myself sick about an operation. I googled the pictures at my desk, which was stupid, they were horrible.

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): I hear you, but I'm not booking any operation. What I am arranging is bloods, a full blood count and liver functions, and an ultrasound of the upper abdomen to look at the gallbladder. Reception will book those for this week.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): This week is better, I've got leave on Thursday. Do I need to starve for the bloods? I had a coffee this morning already, one, with milk and no sugar, I hope that doesn't spoil it.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): For these bloods you don't need to starve, the coffee is fine. The scan sees stones well but it isn't perfect, so a normal one doesn't fully close the door. Cut back hard on the fatty meals, the braai and the vetkoek, smaller plain meals, and keep the Gaviscen for when it flares. If the pain runs over about six hours, or you vomit and can't keep fluids down, or you turn yellow, go to casualty, don't wait.
[SEG0037] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure the diet actually happens. She doesn't listen to me at home.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I will try, promise. Those tuck shop pies smell lekker, but I'll pack a lunch from tomorrow.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in two weeks with the results, normal or not. The rooms will send the booking times.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, ok. If the weekend is quiet do I still come? Sorry, I waffle, my colleagues tease me for it.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): You still come either way. If it flares before then, use the Gaviscen and those casualty rules. We'll talk the tests through when I see you.

spec.situation: Woman with right-upper stomach pain after fatty meals, lasting hours, once with vomiting; takes antacid; mother had gallbladder surgery; blood tests and ultrasound planned.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
